statement: The derivative of a function of a single variable at a chosen input value, when it exists, is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function at that point, serving as the best linear approximation of the function near that input value and quantifying the instantaneous rate of change of the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable. In higher dimensions, the total derivative of a function $f$ from an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ at $\mathbf{a}$ is the unique linear transformation $f'(\mathbf{a})\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ such that $\lim_{\mathbf{h} \to 0} \frac{\lVert f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) - (f(\mathbf{a}) + f'(\mathbf{a})\mathbf{h})\rVert}{\lVert \mathbf{h}\rVert} = 0$.

symbols.meaning: Jacobian matrix composed of partial derivatives (\partial f_i / \partial x_j)_{ij}

properties.property: The total derivative can be represented as the Jacobian matrix $\operatorname{Jac}_{\mathbf{a}} = \left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{ij}$
properties.why: the function $f$ is expressed in terms of coordinate functions $(f_1, f_2, \dots, f_m)$

properties.property: If the total derivative exists at $\mathbf{a}$, then all partial and directional derivatives exist at $\mathbf{a}$, with $f'(\mathbf{a})\mathbf{v}$ giving the directional derivative in direction $\mathbf{v}$
properties.why: the total derivative considers all directions at once as the best linear approximation

properties.property: If all partial derivatives exist and are continuous at $\mathbf{x}$, the directional derivative in direction $\mathbf{v}$ is $D_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}$
properties.why: the continuous partial derivatives determine the variation along any direction

properties.property: For a vector-valued function $\mathbf{y}(t) = (y_1(t), \dots, y_n(t))$, the derivative is the tangent vector $\mathbf{y}'(t) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{\mathbf{y}(t+h)-\mathbf{y}(t)}{h}$ whose coordinates are the derivatives of the coordinate functions
properties.why: coordinate functions are real-valued functions to which differentiation applies componentwise

properties.property: The derivative of a constant function is zero, meaning antiderivatives of $f$ differ by an arbitrary constant $c$
properties.why: constants have zero rate of change with respect to inputs

properties.property: Higher-order derivatives represent repeated differentiation, where the $n$-th derivative $f^{(n)}$ is the derivative of the $(n-1)$-th derivative
properties.why: the differentiation process can be applied iteratively to differentiable functions

assumptions.assumption: The limit defining the derivative or total derivative exists
assumptions.breaks_when: The function is not differentiable at the evaluated point

assumptions.assumption: All partial derivatives exist and are continuous at $\mathbf{x}$ for the directional derivative formula $D_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}$
assumptions.breaks_when: One or more partial derivatives fail to exist or are discontinuous at $\mathbf{x}$

assumptions.assumption: The real derivative is complex linear for functions from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{C}$
assumptions.breaks_when: The Cauchy-Riemann equations between the partial derivatives are not satisfied

failure_modes.signature: The limit of the difference quotient does not exist
failure_modes.cause: The function lacks differentiability at that point

failure_modes.mode: Failure of complex differentiability despite real differentiability
failure_modes.signature: Function is differentiable as a map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ but fails to have a complex derivative
failure_modes.cause: The real derivative is not complex linear because Cauchy-Riemann equations do not hold

failure_modes.mode: Directional derivatives failing to capture full multi-variable behavior
failure_modes.signature: Single directional derivatives exist along individual axes but fail to give a complete picture of function behavior
failure_modes.cause: For $n > 1$, no single directional derivative captures behavior across all directions simultaneously, requiring the total derivative
